utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. All the accused are here. I only notice the absence of Mr. Krgovic. The Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. I think we can start. Who is going to address the Chamber on those three issues that you mentioned, Mr. Haynes, yesterday? Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been speaking to my friend Mr. Meek this morning, and for now it will be just two issues, I think. We're going to talk about the issue, it's primarily his interest during the break, and hopefully resolve our issue, and if we can't, at least I think if there is any argument later, it will be shorter because we'll narrow what's in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all very vague to me for the time being. So who is going first? But are you addressing the Chamber now or after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm here to respond -- I thought Your Honour had asked them to respond to our motion to add another witness, and that's why I'm here. I think the motion was fairly clear, and I'm ready to respond to anything, and I just ask my friends be mindful about when it might be necessary to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends. I would like to say something about our correspondence and our attempts to cooperate with the Prosecutor with regard to the materials that concern the demographics experts or witnesses. I would like to go back and remind the Trial Chamber about the discussion that we had on the 14th of December, 2007, on pages 19238 to 19300, about the character of the witnesses Ewa Tabeau and Mr. Parsons. To this very day we are not certain whether these two witnesses come as experts or just ordinary witnesses. Given the fact that we are about to receive the reports, the [indiscernible] report of the ICMP has already been delivered to us on the 3rd of January, 2008, and the second report we received on the 7th of January of 2008, whereas the report by Mrs. Tabeau we received on the 11th of January, 2008. In order for us to prepare adequately, from the 5th of December we started corresponding with our learned friends from the Prosecutor's office about the delivery of materials that are necessary to us for all this. We received a very short answer yesterday, saying that they are in discussion with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was new to us. This was new to us, that any of these documents could be treated as per Rule 70. The second thing that concerns the other information from the Prosecutor's database, yesterday I was briefed in the whole way by my learned friend from the Prosecutor's office. We are going to try and deal with this as soon as possible without the intervention on the part of the Trial Chamber, if possible, but I would like to inform you that as far as preparation for these two witnesses are concerned, we do not have ample material and we do not have good enough cooperation on the part of the Prosecution in order for us to be prepared for these two very complex witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anybody else wishes to add? Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I agree with my colleague, Madam Nikolic. I've also been attempting to get these documents that Mr. McCloskey claims they promised the government of Bosnia they wouldn't turn over, but I don't know any legal basis, actually, and I guess we're still waiting to hear from Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you wish to address this item? Yes, Madam Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to add something to what my friends have stated. All the documentation that we have received so far, with regard to Mrs. Tabeau's and Mr. Parsons' testimony we received only in English. None of the things have been translated, and we have been told that Mr. Parsons' report is still pending. Given the time restrictions for the Prosecution case, we can see that the translation will not be forthcoming in due time for our clients to be informed about the contents of the future testimony of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One of the conditions of accepting both of you as counsel for your client is that you understand English, so go through it in English and then give the necessary information to your client. Yes, who else? Any further comments, Mr. Nicholls or Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just briefly. Mr. President, regarding the demographics material, just to be clear, that is all available to the Defence, always has been. The issue has been, especially from Mr. Meek, their expert is out of town, and so they wanted some of that material to be able to be sent to him, is my understanding, and we identified what particular material they're interested in. And I am now -- and it's a smaller version than, for example, the massive Bosnian census that is a very sensitive document that cannot be sent out. What they want is a smaller list, and so we've now, to try to meet their needs, have gone to Bosnia to say, "Look, this is a smaller thing. What is the problem with giving that to them?" And I'm hoping we'll be successful. But they have it, they can come in and look at it, as all the demographics stuff, but they're trying to send it out to their people, and we're trying to see if we can facilitate that. But of course we have the interests of Bosnia and their confidential concerns for this kind of information in mind. And I don't think I need to remind the Court, but this is our last-minute response to this DNA issue based on their extremely last-minute challenge to Mr. Manning's use of the DNA after this material was not challenged by Mr. -- in Mr. Brunborg's report. So we're really, as you know, caught off-guard here with this last-minute challenge, but we're working together with them and we're trying to get this done, and I hope these witnesses will be very short and not very complicated. Though since it's science, it may be considered expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other point made by Ms. Nikolic and which is also not clear in our mind until now is whether you're offering these two witnesses as ordinary witnesses or as expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They have reports, they're talking about science. Their opinions are probably going to be asked for briefly. So they're probably, technically, experts. We have an expert, Brunborg, that's relying on their expert reports, so I think they would be experts. We also have the Parsons report in B/C/S now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Whether or not counsel and co-counsel have to speak English, I don't believe that we've had adequate time, on the Parsons report, to even get it to my expert if they intend to call them next week. Number 2, as you'll recall, it was Ewa Tabeau and an unknown person, someone from the IC --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For some time it was like that and we discussed that on the 14th of December, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In addition, I would just add one final comment to Mr. McCloskey's statement, and that would simply be that we really had no idea that the Office of the Prosecutor was relying solely on the ICMP DNA reports for minimum numbers, the MNIs, and not their experts who had been called who he had adequate time to cross-examine until he made that statement during Dean Manning's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Any further -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I have to say relates more to the 65 ter witness application, but does apply to the ICMP issue. And let me make it clear, certainly the ICMP issue has nothing to do with my client's case, and the witness clearly directly has nothing to do with his case and probably indirectly has nothing to do with his case. My observation is simply as follows: The Prosecution have filed the confidential motion, but have made no reference to the time issue. Clearly, the first thing, in my submission, this Chamber needs to decide is whether to extend the length of the Prosecution case. At this moment in time, I'm making no submission about that, but what I do contend is that in order to proceed further, that is what the Court really needs to address, because if the Court is not willing to extend the time for the Prosecution case, then all of these discussions are absolutely pointless, a complete waste of time, because we are going to run out of time on the 1st of February. So, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think I made myself clear last time that we were not cutting down on the time you requested for the cross-examination of the current witness, but that meant that if we over-spilled over the 1st of February, the other dates fixed for the Rule 98 bis submissions were not going to move. So we made that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me. What I thought is the Court had made it clear that the date of the 1st of February wasn't going to shift. If I misunderstood that, then I apologise, and at this moment in time I'm not addressing the timetabling issue. I might ask to be heard on that at some later point, but clearly the Chamber needs first to decide whether it's going to accede to the Prosecution's application. And I've made my position on that clear. Others are going to address it, and I simply support what they have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it was clear enough, Mr. Josse. We were granting -- granted you all the time, 35 hours that you had requested for the cross-examination of this witness, it would have been humanly impossible to then finish the Prosecution case by the 1st of February. But we also wanted to make it clear that if we went beyond that, the other dates were not going to shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed. I now understand that. The Chamber is saying that the Prosecution case can go on the week after next; is that what it amounts to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what's going to happen. Maybe tomorrow Mr. McCloskey comes and renounces the next two or three witnesses. How do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll face that and pronounce ourselves on it at the right moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Excuse me if I've been impertinent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, not at all, Mr. Josse. I wish everyone -- if that is impertinence, I wish everyone would limit himself or herself to that limit. So any further remarks on this? Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two more words, Your Honours, to clarify some things. When Mr. McCloskey says, on page 4, lines 10 and 11, that the material is available to us and it has always been, it is true that it exists in the database of the demographic department of the Prosecutor's office. In order for us to be able to deal with this information, our experts should be able to work in the Prosecutor's office, which is impossible. This material has to be disclosed to us if we're at all given a chance to be prepared for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that disposes, for the time being, of one of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me clarify it. So one is translated already. Well, I told you, Madam Tapuskovic, that you're supposed to know, at least one of you, to be fluent in English and to understand English, and you can -- because the circumstances, are we talking of demographic statistics? There is a time constraint, and we are not to be interpreted as saying that these documents should not be translated. But in the meantime, I mean, just go through them and have consultations with your clients within the shortest possible time. Now, that's okay. Now, which is the other matter that you're coming back to us with after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It will be an issue regarding Witness -- the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said last time that there was a possibility of a stipulation with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That fell through, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yeah. One clarification is that I think my colleague has indicated that there was no B/C/S translation of the transcript, it says in the record, but I think it was the expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, if it's of the transcript, it's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But we've not even received it in English. Apparently it is in B/C/S. Our clients can review it. But any other documents they rely on, under the rules, our clients have an absolute right to have that in their language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've never denied that right. Anyway, you check amongst yourselves what you have and what you don't, I mean, and then we take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The reports have been disclosed in English, and I believe both of them now in B/C/S, from what Ms. Stewart tells me, so I don't think we have a problem there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So who is going to address the Prosecution motion of the 22nd January to add a further witness? I'm not going to mention his name because I don't know if he will be a protected witness or not. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I can't see anybody else jumping to their feet, so I'll do it. I wasn't, until a few moments ago, aware that Mr. Josse was going to raise the brief submission that he did, and I'm sorry if this is a little bit repetitive, but let's be realistic. There are five and a half working days left before the scheduled close of the Prosecution case, and we're partway into the third of seven substantial cross-examinations of the present witness. There are four witnesses of real substance left to be called, three of whom have been added since the start of December, when the Prosecution knew full well what it had to achieve and in what time it had to achieve it. There are substantial legal issues to be determined within the body of the Prosecution case. These include the outstanding 92 bis motion and the threatened 92 quater motion. Realistically, the Prosecution's case not only cannot finish on the 1st of February, there is every likelihood it will run beyond the scheduled date for the 98 bis submissions. The Prosecution does not seek to extend the deadline in its current or any motion, and the only practical suggestion that appears to be made as to how we should fit things within the time is a repeated suggestion that the cross-examination of Richard Butler should be limited. Since the order of the Court as to the deadline for the completion of the Prosecution case, there appears to have been no efforts made to prune, edit, or comply with the order of the Court. And through the motion currently made, the Prosecution now seeks to prolong, presumably on assumption that the Court will extend the deadline or limit

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: is no prejudice to the Defence in any way at all. In any event, the substance of this opposition is this: Every accused person is entitled to know the case they have to face from the outset of the trial, and they're entitled to prepare their and conduct their defence accordingly. And the procedures and the rules of this Tribunal ensure that. The indictment should map out the particular allegations that an accused has to meet. Pre-trial briefs should particularise the Prosecution case, and witness summaries and statements served in support should show the evidentiary basis for each allegation raised in the indictment. You might think all of this is particularly important in a seven-accused case, where each accused is entitled to regard allegations in the indictment and evidence as affecting others and not him. Granted, it is necessarily part of the Prosecution's case that many Serbian VRS military personnel are incapable of belief, but where we are going with this particular corner of the indictment, I simply do not know. I would just remind you of paragraphs 38.1 and 30.10 in the indictment, which, as I read it, does not allege any participation by any member of the Zvornik Brigade at Kozluk on the 15th of July. If there is any ambiguity in those paragraphs, I would simply invite you to look at paragraphs 336 to 338 of the pre-trial brief. At the start of this case, the allegations surrounding the alleged execution at Kozluk was supported by Witness 128, and that was the case my client had to meet. The summary of Witness 128's evidence I invite you to consider. But to draw you quickly to the point, it was said to be relevant only to the cases of Popovic and Nikolic. During the course of Witness 128's testimony before this Tribunal, in fact I think notice of this first came from his proofing note, two further names came to light. I'll be careful not to mention them, because I can't remember which one of the two was a protected witness and which one was not. There was a good deal of excitement about what they might say, but in the event their evidence about who was involved in the executions was neutral, and so the investigative chain went on. Up until this point, I have allowed the evidence about Kozluk to go substantially unchallenged. It was not said at the start of the case materially to affect my client, and the evidence which we heard from the three witnesses who dealt with the subject took the matter no further. Whilst I accept the generality of the indictment, it didn't seem to me that it was or would be the Prosecution's case that Zvornik Brigade soldiers, the security officers, are part responsible for committing executions in Kozluk on the 15th of July. I do not see any application to amend the indictment. What the Prosecution seeks to do through the calling of this witness at the very death of its case is to turn its case in relation Kozluk completely on its head and overturn by contradiction the previous evidence the Court has heard and the allegations in the indictment and the pre-trial brief and the witness summaries which were served at the start of the case. The prejudice lies to my client in my having conducted his case on the basis that I had proper notice of what allegations he faced and what evidence supported them. This of course could easily be cured by the simple expedient of recalling all three of the previous witnesses for further cross-examination who dealt with the question of Kozluk. But as a practical proposition, that is ridiculous. We have only five and a bit days left of the Prosecution case, or a little bit more if you allow it. And so that I'm absolutely clear, I have absolutely no intention of calling Witness 128, Protected Witness 101, or anybody else who has given evidence on this issue as part of my defence case, and it would be utterly unjust to compel me to do so. Being realistic, given the competing interests in relation to Kozluk, it is almost inconceivable that during the course of the Defence case, this issue will not be revisited and provoke -- and provide the Prosecution with the opportunity to call this witness in rebuttal, should they wish to do so. Turning to a further issue, at the start of this case the Trial Chamber made certain rulings about the timetabling of the disclosure of identities and information relating to protected witnesses, and, in general terms, that amounted to this: That their identities should be released to the Defence at least 30 days before they gave evidence. In relation to this witness, I say this: There is no material in the motion, or supporting material, which would support the making of any protective measures. Generally, we've not been obstructive about this, but the request for confidentiality, especially given the tight timetabling concerning this witness's identity, is particularly restrictive and a further ground for refusing the substantive application to add his name to the 65 ter list. It amounts to this: Not only does the Prosecution want to change its case on this issue at the 11th hour and 59th minute, they want to do it in a way that shuts the Defence out forever from investigating the truth and accuracy of what this witness might say. And he might, for all we know, be one of the witnesses who Mr. McCloskey termed at the start of this case a bald-faced liar. There are certainly concerns that many of us have, having listened to the CD of his evidence, as to the sort of person he might be, but as things presently stand the application is that he be here, that we not be allowed to disclose his identity to anybody, even to our investigators, as I understand it, and he be called to give evidence within a matter of a few days. Those are my objections to this application. I submit it's too late and utterly unjust to permit the Prosecution to add this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: While the issue of this witness doesn't have anything to do with my client, on principle, I absolutely support my colleague Mr. Haynes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The issue for Your Honours, I think, to decide, taking into account all of the allegations made by Mr. Haynes and the stage of the case, is whether it would be in the interests of justice for Your Honours to hear this evidence, whether it would help you arrive at a true and just verdict. The threshold first, which Mr. Haynes hasn't addressed particularly, and I suppose he concedes it is: Is the evidence probative, is it relevant on its prima facie face value, is it something that would be useful to you? And I think that relying on my pleadings, I suggest that it is completely. As far as the lateness of the application or the time of the application, I could say, I'd like to address that, if I may, in private session, because to address it fully I need to talk about other -- other facts which are -- should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It can't be said with any credibility, reading the indictment, that this witness changes the case in any significant way. Mr. Pandurevic has always been charged specifically in the indictment with the events in Rocevic and Kozluk. The indictment states that VRS and/or MUP were taking part of -- or taking part in this operation. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it's the right time to go into that, neither on your part, nor on Mr. Haynes' part, what Mr. Pandurevic is charged with, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The whole issue is whether there is justification for accepting your application to have this witness added or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was trying to address, Your Honour, is that there is no prejudice, no significant prejudice, when you're doing your balance of the new information. You have to take, of course, into account the rights of the accused, a very important consideration, and on balance I'll leave it at that. The case has not changed significantly in any way. It's not a complex, new issue, and there is no new charges is what I would say. The second point my friend made about how we've attempted to shut them down and prevent their defence is simply nonsense. It's very likely that the witness we seek to add will ask for protective measures. The Court's recognised before that the protective measures can be completely nullified in advance if that person, who might be a witness, his name is released and spread around. What our motion asks for is simply what the Courts have granted in the past, which is that it not be released to third parties and the public. That doesn't mean investigators. It means nobody, as part of the team, nobody -- their clients, of course, can have that, their team can have it. What it means is we do not want it published to the public. And it's very clear from the motion, which my friend ignored, that we just ask that if there is a reason, a valid reason, why it needs to be released, that they -- that Your Honours are approached and given that. That way, we know that there's been a valid reason, if there's a valid reason to investigate, and that can be done, as we've said before, on an ex parte basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question. We've had witnesses testify about the Kozluk -- alleged Kozluk executions, and we have had at least one, if not more, one witness testify about Pandurevic's return to Zvornik by the afternoon of the 15th of July of 1995. We have also evidence which identifies several persons that allegedly took part in the Kozluk events. What is this witness going to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I go into private session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we hear Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll respond very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, and very briefly, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I believe the first indication that such a source existed was several years ago in the interview of the first witness who gave evidence about this topic. Mr. Nicholls has failed completely to address the question of prejudice, and I do remind you that you set the benchmark for what is fair notice of a witness's identity at the start of this trial; 30 days. And Mr. Nicholls personally has accorded that privilege, I think, certainly to the Nikolic team and others on several occasions throughout this trial when they have complained of lack of due notice of a witness's identity and wish for time to investigate the matter. And I'll pick one example straight out. PW-108 was put back and back and back so that it was seen as fair that the Nikolic team were ready to cross-examine him. This witness, we will get really no effective notice of, and that is a very real prejudice and it simply has not been addressed by Mr. Nicholls. I'll address the issue of probity. The point I made about the indictment is about the probative value of this evidence. I say it doesn't take matters any further, but what it does do is take it in a direction that nobody was expecting to have to meet, and I say that makes it lacking in probity. And those are the three points I wish to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please move into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly, Your Honour, without going into -- into private session, Mr. Haynes talked about early mention of the source. It's always been followed up as much as possible. What I said in private session I think shows the diligence as soon as there was anything to go on. Many of the names, responding to my friend Ms. Nikolic, mentioned have been talked about before, and now there's been a lot of discussion about whether I've portrayed the facts accurately and whether -- whether this -- I think you should look at the interview to decide whether or not you think this is valuable. I don't know if there's any objection to that - it's about 40 pages - because there's been a discussion of what was in it and what was said and what wasn't said, and it may be useful to you if you feel that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come back to you on both issues at a later point in time. In the meantime, let's bring in Mr. Butler, please, and proceed with your cross-examination, Mr. Bourgon, and conclude it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon is going to conclude his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions for you this morning, following which I do not believe it will be necessary to go into the hypothetical which I announced yesterday. At paragraph 5.17 of your revised narrative, you conclude that the removal of the refugee population from Potocari was completed by 2000 hours on the 13th of July. Your conclusion was made on the basis of a report which was filed. My question is: Since drafting your narrative more than five years ago, did you come across any additional material or were you given or provided material by the Office of the Prosecution which would lead you to modify this conclusion? Paragraph 5.17, if you have your report with you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not aware of other documentary evidence which would reflect a different time. I don't know whether or not any witnesses or other individuals may have provided information that it's a different time, so this is the information that I'm aware of. I'm not aware of any contrary information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to my next question, and for this one I would like to refer to the existing situation in the Zvornik Brigade on 12 and 13 July of 1995. And you will recall at a time when the chief of staff, Major Obrenovic, is the senior officer on the ground and in the absence of the brigade commander. And the situation I would like to refer to, just so we're on the same page, refers to the time when he is getting information from Vukotic, the intelligence officer, as well as from other sources regarding the column or elements thereof which are approaching the Zvornik area. Can you identify the period that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the basis of your analysis of the material at your disposal, I take it you can confirm that during this period, Major Obrenovic is scrambling to organise preparations for the arrival of the column. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he's actively working to muster whatever remaining military forces there are within the brigade that can be pulled off the front lines, and other reserve forces, in order to put a blocking force in place for the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you can confirm that on the basis of your analysis, in part due to the absence of resources deployed with Tactical Group 1, and despite the fact, as you say, that he's drawing resources from the battalions, that at this point in time he is short of personnel and especially short of experienced officers to organise preparations for the arrival of the column; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is short personnel in respect to having experienced combat and infantry fighters, and he is short officers with the battalions, and that as a result he's having to use his own brigade staff operations officers to, in effect, go down and be platoon and company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question in this regard or my next question deals with your observation, and that is at paragraph 7.9 of your report, and it then appears again at paragraph 10.15 of your revised narrative. I should have said "revised narrative" the first time around. Both paragraphs are from the revised narrative, where you note that on the 13th of July, 1995, at approximately 2300 hours, Drago Nikolic would have been replaced as forward command post IKM brigade duty officer by Major Galic. Do you have this paragraph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Butler, you would agree with me, and I think this has been mentioned before, but I could not find the reference, that the replacement of the brigade forward command post duty officer, especially in the situation that we are referring to here, is a decision which normally requires the approval of either the commander or the senior officer on the ground; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree. I mean, it would have required either Colonel Pandurevic or Major Obrenovic to make that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, although the Defence position has been contrary, looking at your narrative and to some evidence adduced in this trial, it would appear that in fact Major Obrenovic himself would have approved the replacement of Drago Nikolic, and you would not be surprised by this fact, would you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe, from my knowledge of statements that the individual has provided to the Office of the Prosecutor, that he in fact does confirm that he is the person who authorised the replacement of Drago Nikolic at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I did, and I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, according to further evidence adduced in this trial, it would appear that Major Obrenovic would have approved a replacement of Drago Nikolic without verifying who was the next officer on the list or who was available, and that in fact he only learned much later that it was Major Galic who would have replaced Drago Nikolic that night. That's the evidence we've heard in this trial, and on this basis -- and of course taking into account your military knowledge and experience, I suggest to you that this is not what you would expect from an experienced VRS officer responsible for a brigade in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, under the context of the circumstances, the fact that Major Obrenovic would have authorised the relief of Drago Nikolic, again that's within his competence to do. Under normal circumstances, the officer who is being relieved has the responsibility to ensure that his relief has arrived prior to him officially departing. Whether or not Major Obrenovic would have specifically designated which officer to go and relieve him or whether or not that is a decision that he would have left to the operations people is a matter of speculation. I mean, it would not -- the circumstances you described are not unusual, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the situation or the part of the question I am referring to is, you said it yourself, that because he was short of experienced personnel, he had to use his own officers and deploy them for combat activities. My question to you is: In such circumstances, is it normal that he will authorise the replacement of Drago Nikolic without even knowing who will replace Drago Nikolic and who is available to replace Drago Nikolic? And I'm asking this in your capacity as -- on the basis of your military experience.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, under the circumstances, I mean, the fact that he had to do that was an anomaly. However, that's, you know, what happens in that particular situation within the shortage of officers. It doesn't mean that Drago Nikolic is still not responsible for ensuring his relief is in place and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's not my question, Mr. Butler. My question is very simple. You're supposed to be someone with military experience. Would you have expected Major Obrenovic to verify and to hand-pick whoever was going to replace Drago Nikolic to ensure that he would have the right resources to do the job that he has to do at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, to the first part of your question, I would have expected that Major Obrenovic would have verified that the position was filled. I don't believe that within the context of the operations staff, that it would have been necessary for Major Obrenovic to hand-pick the next duty officer. That could have very easily been a decision delegated to the operations people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I suggest to you it would have been necessary for him to know who is going so that who is remaining available for his activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that as a matter of information, that Major Obrenovic would have wanted to know who it was at some point, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's all I was looking for. I'm moving to the next question, which deals with the arrival of a large number of prisoners in the area of Zvornik. It would appear, on the basis of evidence adduced in this trial, that Major Obrenovic, in his capacity as senior officer of the brigade at the time, would have been informed of this situation - I'm talking about the arrival of a large number of prisoners - for the first time in the early evening of 13 July. That's the evidence we've heard in this case. And I take it you're familiar that this -- you can confirm this fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm familiar with this as the evidence that has come forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Again, the next question has to do with your military experience. Pursuant to further evidence heard during this trial, it would appear that during a telephone conversation with General Zivanovic, which took place shortly after being informed of the arrival of a large group of prisoners and being informed that this group of prisoners would subsequently be killed in the area of Zvornik, Major Obrenovic did not mention this situation, nor consider it appropriate to engage his superior on this issue. That's the evidence we've heard. On the basis of your military knowledge and experience, I suggest that this is not what you would expect from an experienced VRS officer responsible for a brigade in these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to paragraph 7.27 of your narrative, in which you conclude, towards the end of this paragraph, and you have your report with you, I believe, I quote - it's one short sentence: "Late on the 15th, all burial activity was completed at the Orahovac site." Do you have this quote?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question is the following: Since drafting your narrative more than five years ago, did you come across any additional information or were you given any additional material which would lead you to modify this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that in the intervening period, that the OTP has interviewed a number of the engineer operators, but as far as I understand the events that occurred there, the actual burial operations were done by the 15th and that subsequent to that, on the morning of the 16th, equipment was being -- any equipment that was left over was being moved out. I don't have any information that they were still burying bodies on 16 July at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question relates to events which would have taken place in Orahovac on the 14th and 15th of July, and that is as described in your narrative in Chapter 7, pages 63 to 68. So the Orahovac situation in general. In paragraph 7.6, you conclude, and I quote: " ... That survivor testimony and documents from the Zvornik Brigade indicate that elements of the brigade command, the Engineer Company, the Military Police Company, and elements of (at least) the 4th Infantry Battalion, were all involved in the planning, detention, execution, and subsequent burial of Muslim men at the Orahovac site." I'd like to have in e-court, please, 65 ter 3D133, which is in tab 3 in your binder. Are you familiar with this document, Mr. Butler, which is an indictment against four members of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade who are charged for participating in the mistreatment, beatings, cruel treatment, and acts causing terror at the Orahovac school on 14 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It should be in tab 3.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have it. I believe I have seen an English language version of this, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you have an English version of the indictment with you in your binder?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this document confirms the involvement of the Bratunac Military Police Company in the Orahovac events, and that, as such, it could modify your conclusion in paragraph 7.6?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect, an indictment confirms nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I agree, and I will correct the language I've used. It would be an indicator that at least there is some evidence of members of the Bratunac Military Police Company involved in the events in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree. I believe that information that has come to light in the last couple of years has -- does in fact reflect that members of the Bratunac Brigade military police were escorting prisoner convoys to more than just the location that I identify from documents in Pilica. I believe they've now been identified at both Orahovac and Petkovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree, in this regard, that the involvement in the Orahovac events, and maybe more, as you say, of elements from a brigade other than Zvornik, is both a significant and important fact to take into account in analysing these events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a factor that should be taken into account in analysing the events. The importance of it is entirely dependent upon what their activities were at the time. The fact that -- you know, in the abstract, that a police patrol or group of police individuals, or even soldiers from Bratunac, may have escorted a convoy up does not replace or supplant the involvement of the Zvornik Brigade in that particular crime base. So while it is a factor to be considered, certainly, one would have to look at the actual activities involved to determine how much of a factor it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my point is simply that the fact that this is from an external brigade or another brigade and the fact that these people are military police, these --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are factors, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move to my last issue, which deals with Chapter 1 of your narrative, and in this chapter you address the historical background. I refer you to paragraph 1.3. That should be on page 6-7 of the -- of your narrative or revised narrative, where you describe how a conflict erupted in Zvornik in the early evening -- sorry, the reference might be wrong in the transcript. I was referring to pages 6 and 7 and not 67. So paragraph 1.3, you describe how a conflict erupted in Zvornik in the early evening hours of 8 April 1992, and that would be when, as you say, elements of the JNA 336th Motorised Brigade, Arkan's Serbian volunteers -- volunteer guards, and local SDS or SDS-backed TO units, seized control of the predominantly Muslim-populated town. Do you have this paragraph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: According to your description, this attack was preceded by an ultimatum issued several hours earlier to Zvornik SDA representatives at the Hotel Jesero in Mali Zvornik. According to what you say, during this meeting Arkan and local SDS officials demanded the surrender of the town. What I'd like to refer you to is what you say in paragraph 1.3 concerning the presence of Captain Dragan Obrenovic at this meeting, and my first question is: Is this the same Dragan Obrenovic who became the chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There are two documents you refer to in support of your conclusion that Dragan Obrenovic was present. Both of them are referred to in your revised narrative. The first one, footnote 7, and you have this in tab 30 in your binder. If you can just take a look at this document, and this is document 5D458 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You have it, okay. Without reading all of it, you recall this document which you footnoted in your revised narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second document was referred to in footnote 6, and that was a letter addressed to General Jankovic, commander of the Tuzla Corps, by a person called Izet Mehinagic who was present at the meeting. That is in tab 47 of your binder, if you can have a look at this, and if I can have in e-court 65 ter number 733. This one is short, and I would like, Mr. Butler, to have you read this one-page letter, and then I will ask you one question on this basis.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe what document 733 is, what this letter is, your analysis of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular letter was, as described, a letter from the individual Izet Mehinagic, and I hope I've pronounced that correctly, to General Savo Jankovic, who was at that time the commander of the JNA 17th Corps, requesting protection in some effect by the JNA in order to prevent the conflict that was looming with respect to Zvornik. He lays out the -- at least a short version, he lays out the fact that, you know, a meeting occurred in Mali Zvornik and who the participants were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my question to you is: On the basis of your analysis of this document, the previous document, which was the one you saw before that at tab 33, as well as any other material you may have seen in drafting your report, were you able to conclude that on that occasion, Dragan Obrenovic was arrested by Arkan in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. All the evidence that I'm aware of, outside of his own statements, of course, reflects that he was a willing participant in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This concludes, Mr. President, my cross-examination, but I have one clarification I would like to bring, which is: After reading the transcript yesterday, I may have put my question in a wrong way. That was page 3 in the transcript yesterday. And I would just like to read you the question, Mr. Butler, and ask you to clarify whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The question at that time was that: "In light of these duties and responsibilities of the intelligence officer, I take it you will agree with me that this officer works, of course, in the Operations Department of the Command Staff." I would just like to confirm. Maybe my question wasn't clear. At least I wasn't sure. But you will agree with me that the intelligence officer, of course, is not subordinated to the operations officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, he is subordinated to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I wanted to do by this question is to highlight the fact that he was on the operations side of the house. That's what I meant, and I believe that's how you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Let's have the break now, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So who is going next? Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's me, Your Honour, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. If you could introduce yourself to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Butler. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic. I represent Mr. Borovcanin in this case. Before I start putting questions to you, I would like to tell you first that Mr. Borovcanin's Defence by and large accepts your positions about the resubordination of the police to the VRS Army. However, a certain number of answers to the previous questions calls for additional clarification, and I'm going to ask you questions in that sense. I would like to start with the 14th January 2008 and the answer that you provided on page 19633 to the question as to how cooperation differs from coordination/cooperation, and then you answered this: [In English] "So when you have a situation, for example, where the army staff and the police staff have dictated, you know, how particular units can be used or under what parameters that they can be used, within the framework of those guidance from the senior commanders on both sides, the lower units are going to be expected to collaborate to ensure that they accomplish that mission." [Interpretation] This was your answer, you will remember, I'm sure. I would like to ask you this: Am I right and did I understand you well, that your position that the staffs of the police forces and the staffs of the military forces decided together on how to use the police and military units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, if you're referring to the staffs of the police forces and the staffs of the military forces at the highest level, the equivalent of the Main Staff and, I guess -- and police had a staff as well, no, they don't coordinate at that particular level. What their function is is once they set the parameters by which the police will be engaged in military operations, for example, by assigning police units to a certain military operation for a certain military time, they're finished with it to that extent. What happens at the lower level is when that particular police unit shows up, it is incumbent upon that lower-level commander to coordinate with the military unit that he's been resubordinated to, you know, in order to be fully integrated into the plan and the larger defence. But -- so, I mean, that's the thrust of what I'm trying to make with that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that this clarifies your position fully. With regard to this, I wanted to ask you something else. When you were working on this case and as you were preparing your expert analysis, did you ever come across a situation in which a MUP unit would be superior to a military unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't believe that I have; certainly not in 1995. 1992 was a much more chaotic circumstance, and it may have occurred then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Can the witness now please be shown 4D0092. As we're waiting for the document to appear, let me tell you that this is a schematic which was prepared by the Defence and represents the structure of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska based on the Law of Defence in case of war or imminent threat of war. Could you please look at the schematic and tell us whether it corresponds to your understanding of the structure of the armed forces in Republika Srpska, which is based on the law -- on the application of the Law on Defence in a situation of war or an imminent threat of war. Would you be happy with a hard copy of the --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine, sir, and I agree, I think this is an - in a broad framework - accurate reflecting the components of the armed forces and the role of the Supreme Command as the collective decision-making body, but the fact that the RS president is the sole executive authority behind that decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We no longer need this document. Now I would like us to look at P00057. You've already discussed this document at great length on examination-in-chief. This is an order by the chief of the police forces. The number is 64/95, and the date is 10 July 1995. For your better understanding, I would like you to have the law on the application of the Law on the Interior Affairs in a situation of war or an imminent threat of war, which is Exhibit number 4D005725, because I would like to put certain questions to you about the extent to which the first document reflects the law and the legal solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can I have the assistance of Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order says that it was passed pursuant to an order of the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska. I would kindly ask you to look at Article 13, paragraph 1 of the law, which reads that police units participated in combat pursuant to an order of the supreme commander of the armed forces and the Ministry of the Interior. Could you please confirm that precisely Article 13, paragraph 1 of this law provided the president with the authority to issue the order on the use of these forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As we go on, it says in the first paragraph: "In order to break up the enemy force in the protected area of Zenica [as interpreted]." Based on the description in the order, can we then conclude that the unit was sent to combat -- with a combat mission and that this was in keeping with Article 14, paragraph 3, of the law that you have before you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A small correction. Zenica is on the record. I just think we should catch that before ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I said "Srebrenica." I suggest a wrong interpretation. [Interpretation] Thank you very much. And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could give me the exhibit number again of the law. 4D ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's 4DP00725.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now can we look at Article 13 of the law that you have before you, which says the Ministry of the Interior rules the police units through the staff of the command of the police forces of the Ministry. Tell me, please, this order, does it also reflect Article 13, paragraph 2 of the law, bearing in mind, of course, that at the end you can see who the issuer of the order was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is what I was looking at is the fact that in this particular context, Tomislav Kovac is noted as the staff commander, which I take to be the police staff commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. And now can we please look at the order that we have before us still, and can we please look at the heading of the order, which shows the addressees. We can see that the order was sent to the commander of the Special Police Brigade, to the staff of the Trnovo Police Forces Command, to the staff of the Vogosca Police Forces Command, to the staff of the Bijeljina Police Forces Command, to the Zvornik Public Security Centre, to the Sarajevo Public Security Centre, and finally to the Jahorina Police Training Camp. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in three of the addressees. The order was sent to the commander of the Special Police Brigade, it was also sent to the Zvornik Public Security Centre and also to the Jahorina Police Training Camp. Can you confirm that for us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Is it obvious that we are talking about three different components within the Ministry of the Interior, judging by the addressees, and they are all within the sector of public security, obviously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think to be accurate, we're talking about three different areas within the public safety realm, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. Thank you very much. Let us now look at bullet point 1 of this order, which reads a part of the MUP is to be sent as an independent unit to the Srebrenica sector. Can we arrive at the conclusion, if we use the term "independent unit," that this unit was not connected with other MUP units on the ground and that, in practical terms, it was resubordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in -- at a point in time when it arrives, I agree. At this juncture, though, where you're talking about "detach," you know, I agree that at that point, it's under its own independent command for the purpose of detaching from the front and moving there. At the point when it arrives at its destination, and I guess then Colonel Borovcanin reports to, you know, General Krstic, at that time the army assumes command over that formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now can we please look at bullet point 5 of the same order. You have just mentioned this in your previous answer, but let's connect that with Article 14 of the law, which states as follows: "Police units which pursuant to an order of the supreme commander of the armed forces are sent into combat shall be resubordinated to the commander of the unit in whose area of responsibility they are engaged in combat." Is it what the Article 14 says, and is bullet point 5 exactly the reflection of Article 14 of the law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that's -- that's how I read paragraph 5 of this order in this particular light.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, although we have already touched upon that subject, at the very bottom of the document it is stated -- it is stated that the order is sent by the staff commander, so it is beyond dispute that at the time when the order was issued, Mr. Kovac was the deputy Minister of the Interior. However, is my understanding correct when I say that he issued this order as the commander of the Police Forces Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is my understanding, that that is under the authority by which he issued this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now let's look at the Exhibit P00008. This is another order this time issued by Radovan Karadzic, dated 22 April 1995. I am interested in the introductory part of the document. As we can see in the heading of this document, the date is 22nd April 1995, which was sent to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and also to the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior. In the introduction to the order, it says: " ... We were informed about some problems and confusion regarding the engagement of the MUP in combat activities. In order to avoid certain dilemmas or problems, I hereby order ..." And further on, this order explains more precisely how MUP forces may be used for combat. What I wanted to ask you is this: Can we agree that this order, issued by Radovan Karadzic, was obviously a consequence of the former confusion and problems and that the goal of this order was to clarify, in more specific detail, as to how MUP units could be used in such specific situations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I believe that we no longer need this document, and now I would like to look at some very specific examples of how things worked in practice. I would like to have 4D00087 in e-court. You've already seen this document during your examination-in-chief, and I would kindly ask you to keep the law that we have been discussing, which is 4DP00725.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have a document which is a letter of the deputy rear commander, and it concerns full provisions for the MUP unit monitoring the Srebrenica and Bratunac areas. The date indicated on the document is the 15th of July, 1995. You've already had an occasion to see this document, but now I'd kindly ask you to -- the provision of Article 14, paragraph 5 of the law that you have before you, which says that in the area where combat operations are taking place, the commander to whom the police unit is resubordinated will provide logistical support to the police unit as well as to the other units of the Army of Republika Srpska. Could you please find it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it on the ELMO, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And would this be precisely a situation of that sort, where certain dilemmas arise as to who is it that should provide food for the police unit, and this is precisely the kind of situation that is provided for by Article 14, in which it is stated that it should be the commander to whom the unit is resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As a matter of organisation and practice, the police units, while they make, you know, effective combat fighters, they do not have the necessary logistics and other sustainability components of military units that would allow them to remain on their own. In light of that fact, they would, you know, naturally rely on the army to provide the necessary life support over the immediate issue of combat rations, ammunition, medical support, all the other things that a military formation needs in order to sustain itself in combat. So I believe you're correct, what we're seeing here is a natural application of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You must have been reading my mind and anticipated my next question, but let's put things in the context of these events. Can we agree that in the area of Bratunac, Potocari and Srebrenica, the -- Mr. Borovcanin did not have his staff or his headquarters, or whatever we may want to call it, he did not have his own logistics infrastructure, command post facilities, or any such thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have another fact that I would like to put to you with regard to the document that we have just been looking at. The MUP unit that is mentioned in this particular document, and we have to bear in mind that this was on the 15th of July, was not the 1st Company of the PJP Zvornik, it was not the 2nd Detachment of Special Brigade Sekovici, because those two units at that time had already been engaged in the combat in the Baljkovica sector, which is outside the territory of either Srebrenica or Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the context that Colonel Sobot is discussing, he's discussing all of them. At the time this order is issued, and I believe we're talking about roughly, I mean, 10 -- there's a time notation of around 10.00, so I'm not sure exactly when this order was sent and drafted to the Main Staff. But it was at that time that the decisions were made and that those two MUP formations were being sent from the road up to the Zvornik area. So I think in that context, he's talking about obviously supporting all of the MUP forces that are down there, although I can't say that he is aware that, you know, at this purpose, those two units are now going from one position to another. Regardless, you know, it's still the zone of the Drina Corps, and as a result the Drina Corps still, regardless of whether they're in Bratunac or Zvornik, is still going to have to support them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your answer. However, are you contesting the fact that on the 15th, the 1st PJP Company and the Sekovici Detachment were already in Zvornik and in the Baljkovica sector?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I believe that those formations, I mean, their unit commanders were present at Zvornik around noon, where they were at Standard, and I believe the bulk of the formations were in the Zvornik Brigade area by approximately 1500 hours on 15 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. While we were looking at the previous documents, on several occasions the term "Police Forces Staff" came up. I'm asking you, during the analysis of documents, did you come by other documents where the staffs of the police forces were mentioned? Please just say "yes" or "no," and then I'll have my next questions for you with this regard.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not during the construction of the report, I did not have access to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I suppose that this may reduce the need for some questions that I was going to ask you, but let me ask you this: Are you familiar with the staffs, as such, at what level of the MUP, if they existed, and if you know that they did, and what was their purpose and function? Can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- only in the broadest sense that we've just discussed. It was not an area of my particular expertise, to go into the inner workings of the Ministry of the Interior of the RS. My concern, in looking at their involvement, was only with respect to this particular operation and the determination that on the ground level, who the MUP would be responsible to within the context of the crime scene. So I don't believe I have the expertise to go into the broader areas of how the MUP staff works.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You know what, in that case I will only have one more question, and I'm putting to you that in the course of 1995, the staff of the police forces of the MUP did function and did exist. However, I'm interested in something else. At least as of 20th March 1995, up to August 1995, there was also the staff of the police forces in Zvornik with the Public Security Services Centre. I'm putting this to you and I'm asking for your comment on that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am aware, if we're talking about the same things, that within the structure of each CSB, to include Zvornik, there was a small staff that was -- whose job it was was to prepare and, where necessary, deploy the municipal police and manage the activities of what we know as the PJP police companies. That was part of every CSB, as far as I'm aware, if that's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will no longer insist on this question. You said it clearly that this was not part of your expertise, so I will move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can Exhibit number P002204 be put on e-court, please. [In English] It's the wrong number. I apologise. It's P00204.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for this exhibit, let me tell you that this is an order by Colonel Krstic from the Drina Corps of May 1995. I would like to look at the part which says or which indicates who the addressee of the order were. And it says: "To the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment," and so on and so forth, and the last is the Zvornik Public Security Centre. Can you confirm that for us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now can we go to page 3 of this document, bullet point 3, paragraph 3. Here we have a minor problem with the translation, I believe, and that's why I would like to read the original version in B/C/S, which reads: "The MUP company is attached ..." 3, bullet point 3: " ... to the 1st Vlasenica Infantry Brigade, and it is engaged on the attack axis of the 1st Vlasenica Infantry Brigade," and so on and so forth. Can you please confirm this, now that you have heard the interpretation into English. "The MUP company is attached to the 1st Vlasenica Brigade."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean given the context of the rest of the paragraph, I believe the phrase "attachment" would adequately describe the relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And it says further on that it shall be engaged according to the ideas of the commander of the 1st Vlasenica Brigade. This is what it says here, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Roughly, it basically notes the fact that, you know, the MUP will be employed, you know, in the manner that the commander of the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade wants it to be employed on the battlefield. That's a fair reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And let's just elaborate a little. Can it be concluded, from this order, that the brigade commander was the one who made decisions on how to use a company at the moment when it was attached to his unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Within the confines of the guidance that he has already received, and certainly in this context, I mean, that's what it implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to have a look at P00205 [Realtime transcript read in error "P00025"].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Then Colonel Krstic signed this document. The date is the 16th of May, 1995, and that is a supplement to the order that we saw previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There is again one mistake in transcript. The number of the document is P00205.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document, I'm interested in two things. First of all, if you look at the addressees, you will see that there is no mention of CSB Zvornik among the addressees. Can you confirm that for me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2 of this order, we can see mention of the MUP, that is to say, the 1st Vlasenica Infantry Brigade with a MUP company, so on the basis of that we can infer that they're still within the Vlasenica Brigade or, rather, they had been attached to the Vlasenica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to move on to P00208. This is a further elaboration of that order, so generally the situation is the same. However, can we first command -- I beg your pardon. Can we first establish, when we look at the addressees up here, that again there is no reference to the Public Security Centre of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you connecting this particular document with the ones that we talked about in May, because this one has a date of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. What matters to me is the substance of this document or, rather, the one that we had occasion to see previously.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree, in the header data there is no reference here to CSB Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to have a look at paragraph 1 of this document, so the Command of the Vlasenica Infantry Brigade, the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade, the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade in cooperation with the MUP in their areas of responsibility shall take all measures of combat support, control of territory, detect, block and disarm all infiltrated groups. In case they are not able to do so, at the expense of endangering the lives of our troops while disarming them, crash and destroy the groups and do not allow them to link up with the forces active at the front." Have you had a look at this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The 20th of July, this MUP company is still attached to the Vlasenica Brigade, as we can see here; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't read it at all that way. I read this particular paragraph as a direction by General Krstic that the commands of the Vlasenica Brigade, the 2nd Romanija Brigade and the Birac Infantry Brigades will cooperate -- or with the cooperation of the MUP SJB forces, will secure their areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My mistake. I'm sorry, I made the wrong suggestion to you. In relation to this document, I wanted to ask you something else. I do apologise. This does not have to do with the previous matter. I do apologise. I made a mistake. However, what you saw just now, does it show that from the moment when the MUP unit was attached to the military unit, in this specific case this brigade, this military formation commands the unit and no longer informs the MUP about the use of such a unit, up until the moment when this unit returns to the MUP establishment, of course?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree, there would be no requirement, once the MUP formation was attached, to continue to keep the parent formation involved, again the assumption being that the MUP was, in fact, continually employed within the scope and the intent of the initial order. So in that respect, unless the local MUP commander were going to notify his superior, the military would not have a requirement to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was my question, and I do apologise once again if I misled you. Now I would like to move on to another topic. During the examination-in-chief, you gave comments with regard to a few reports -- Dragomir Vasic from the Zvornik Public Security Station. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me that not a single one of these telegrams that we looked at was not -- was sent either to Mr. Borovcanin or the Special Brigade of the police? Can you confirm that for me or would you like to have another look?
